claim: Over 800,000 patients are diagnosed with myocardial infarction per year.
source: For a proportion of the over 800,000 patients diagnosed per year (Benjamin, 2019), excessive hypertrophy and scar formation in the non-infarcted myocardium can result in the development of heart failure, with decreases in contractility, myocardial conductivity, and pump function leading to poor rates of survival (Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Benjamin, 2019.

claim: Excessive hypertrophy and scar formation in the non-infarcted myocardium can result in the development of heart failure.
source: For a proportion of the over 800,000 patients diagnosed per year (Benjamin, 2019), excessive hypertrophy and scar formation in the non-infarcted myocardium can result in the development of heart failure, with decreases in contractility, myocardial conductivity, and pump function leading to poor rates of survival (Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2017.

claim: Currently prescribed therapeutics for MI patients are designed to reduce hypertrophy via several neurohormonal mechanisms including inhibition of angiotensin II (AngII) and norepinephrine (NE) or increasing the bioavailability of natriuretic peptides (NPs).
source: Currently prescribed therapeutics for MI patients are designed to reduce hypertrophy via several neurohormonal mechanisms including inhibition of angiotensin II (AngII) and norepinephrine (NE) or increasing the bioavailability of natriuretic peptides (NPs) (Ponikowski et al., 2016), but no drugs have been approved for treating cardiac fibrosis directly.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ponikowski et al., 2016.

claim: No drugs have been approved for treating cardiac fibrosis directly.
source: Currently prescribed therapeutics for MI patients are designed to reduce hypertrophy via several neurohormonal mechanisms including inhibition of angiotensin II (AngII) and norepinephrine (NE) or increasing the bioavailability of natriuretic peptides (NPs) (Ponikowski et al., 2016), but no drugs have been approved for treating cardiac fibrosis directly.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in the field as of the publication date.

claim: Scar formation serves a reparative function in post-MI wound healing by replacing necrotic myocardium and preventing infarct expansion and cardiac rupture.
source: Notably, scar formation serves a reparative function in post-MI wound healing by replacing necrotic myocardium and preventing infarct expansion and cardiac rupture (Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weber et al., 2013.

claim: Cardiac fibroblasts infiltrate the infarct site and assume an activated, synthetic phenotype to promote matrix accumulation.
source: This balance is mediated largely by cardiac fibroblasts, which infiltrate the infarct site and assume an activated, synthetic phenotype to promote matrix accumulation (Chen and Frangogiannis, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Frangogiannis, 2013.

claim: A wide variety of biochemical factors regulate fibroblast behavior such as AngII, transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ1), endothelin-1 (ET1), and various inflammatory cytokines.
source: A wide variety of biochemical factors regulate fibroblast behavior such as AngII, transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ1), endothelin-1 (ET1), and various inflammatory cytokines (Leask, 2010; Turner, 2014), but a growing body of research has demonstrated that biomechanical factors such as circumferential stretch and tissue stiffness are also critical determinants of fibroblast behavior (Saucerman et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leask, 2010 and Turner, 2014.

claim: Biomechanical factors such as circumferential stretch and tissue stiffness are critical determinants of fibroblast behavior.
source: A wide variety of biochemical factors regulate fibroblast behavior such as AngII, transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ1), endothelin-1 (ET1), and various inflammatory cytokines (Leask, 2010; Turner, 2014), but a growing body of research has demonstrated that biomechanical factors such as circumferential stretch and tissue stiffness are also critical determinants of fibroblast behavior (Saucerman et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saucerman et al., 2019.

claim: Parallel transduction of biochemical and biomechanical stimuli is integrated by fibroblasts through a complex signaling network in which pathways interact via systems-level crosstalk and feedback mechanisms.
source: Parallel transduction of biochemical and biomechanical stimuli is integrated by fibroblasts through a complex signaling network in which pathways interact via systems-level crosstalk and feedback mechanisms (Hinz, 2015; Saraswati et al., 2020), making prediction and control of fibroblast behavior in the post-MI environment highly challenging.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hinz, 2015 and Saraswati et al., 2020.

claim: The extended model includes nine cytokine inputs known to mediate fibroblast activation post-MI as well as mechanical tension.
source: Our extended model includes nine cytokine inputs known to mediate fibroblast activation post-MI as well as mechanical tension, which is transduced via multiple mechanosensors including integrins, stretch-activated ion channels, and the G-coupled protein receptor angiotensin type I receptor (AT1R) (Figure 1, and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for nodes added to the previous network).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model description and references to Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mechanical tension is transduced via multiple mechanosensors including integrins, stretch-activated ion channels, and the G-coupled protein receptor angiotensin type I receptor (AT1R).
source: Our extended model includes nine cytokine inputs known to mediate fibroblast activation post-MI as well as mechanical tension, which is transduced via multiple mechanosensors including integrins, stretch-activated ion channels, and the G-coupled protein receptor angiotensin type I receptor (AT1R) (Figure 1, and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for nodes added to the previous network).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model structure and established knowledge of mechanotransduction pathways.

claim: The total network consists of 109 nodes and 174 reactions.
source: The total network, consisting of 109 nodes and 174 reactions, was implemented as a logic-based ODE model using the open-source Netflux package as previously described (Kraeutler et al., 2010) in which node activity levels and reaction weights are normalized values between 0 and 1 (e.g. an activity of 0.5 represents 50% of maximum activity).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the model structure.

claim: For fibroblast-secreted outputs, simulated responses to biochemical and mechanical stimuli correctly predicted qualitative changes in protein secretion in 81.8% (63/77) of simulations.
source: For fibroblast-secreted outputs, simulated responses to biochemical and mechanical stimuli correctly predicted qualitative changes in protein secretion in 81.8% (63/77) of simulations (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The model correctly predicted qualitative changes in activation levels of canonical signaling intermediates for 80.5% (33/41) of simulations compared to experimental studies.
source: Additionally, the model correctly predicted qualitative changes in activation levels of canonical signaling intermediates for 80.5% (33/41) of simulations compared to experimental studies (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The model predicted increased expression of collagens, matricellular proteins, and protease inhibitors with exposure to canonical agonists TGFβ1, AngII, platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα), and mechanical tension.
source: Consistent with previous studies, the model-predicted increased expression of collagens, matricellular proteins, and protease inhibitors with exposure to canonical agonists TGFβ1, AngII, platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα), and mechanical tension, and secretion of these pro-fibrotic species was accompanied by increased MMP production.
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions consistent with previous studies.

claim: Tension amplified, dampened, or reversed fibroblast responses to individual biochemical cues.
source: We examined the extent and dynamics of mechano-chemo interactions by simulating biochemical dose-response behavior under varying levels of mechanical stimulation, finding that tension amplified, dampened, or reversed fibroblast responses to individual biochemical cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results described in the abstract and results section.

claim: A tension level of 0.5 amplified, dampened, or reversed an average 56.7% of node AUCs toward six biochemical inputs compared to basal levels of tension.
source: Using this threshold, a tension level of 0.5 (i.e. 50% of maximum stimulation) amplified, dampened, or reversed an average 56.7% of node AUCs toward these six inputs compared to basal levels of tension (Figure 3A), and a tension level of 0.9 (i.e. 90% of maximum stimulation) sizably altered an average 60.4% of node AUCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: A tension level of 0.9 sizably altered an average 60.4% of node AUCs.
source: Using this threshold, a tension level of 0.5 (i.e. 50% of maximum stimulation) amplified, dampened, or reversed an average 56.7% of node AUCs toward these six inputs compared to basal levels of tension (Figure 3A), and a tension level of 0.9 (i.e. 90% of maximum stimulation) sizably altered an average 60.4% of node AUCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Moderate tension levels (reaction weights 0.2–0.5) largely amplified the effects of inputs.
source: Within inputs that demonstrated tension-modulated dose-response behavior, the level of tension applied mediated different types of interactions. Moderate tension levels (reaction weights 0.2–0.5) largely amplified the effects of inputs; of the six inputs demonstrating tension-mediated changes in dose-response behavior, 51.8% of node AUCs were amplified at a tension level of 0.5 on average while 4.43% and 0.46% of node AUCs were dampened or reversed on average, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: High levels of tension (reaction weights 0.6–0.9) largely dampened network responses to inputs.
source: High levels of tension (reaction weights 0.6–0.9) largely dampened network responses to these inputs, with 56.4% of nodes on average decreasing AUCs with the same six inputs compared to 2.75% and 1.22% of node AUCs showing sizable amplification or reversal, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: NE-mediated inhibition of procollagen I expression was amplified by tension.
source: These changes in sensitivity were indicative of network interactions between tension and biochemical stimuli; we observed that NE-mediated inhibition of procollagen I expression was amplified by tension (Figure 3C), which can be explained by the logical requirement for tension-induced smad3 activation for effective inhibition by cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Tension-mediated desensitization of procollagen I expression toward TGFβ1 can be explained mechanistically by a common autocrine feedback loop integrating both tension and TGFβ1 signals via a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activator protein 1 (AP1) signaling axis.
source: We also found that tension-mediated desensitization of procollagen I expression toward TGFβ1 can be explained mechanistically by a common autocrine feedback loop integrating both tension and TGFβ1 signals via a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activator protein 1 (AP1) signaling axis (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanistic analysis shown in Figures 3E-F.

claim: 4.40% of nodes reversed the direction of dose-response curves with IL1 stimulation with a tension reaction weight of 0.6 or greater compared to baseline tension levels.
source: Notably, 4.40% of nodes reversed the direction of dose-response curves with IL1 stimulation with a tension reaction weight of 0.6 or greater compared to baseline tension levels, including intermediate nodes involved in TGFβ1 signaling (TGFβ1R, NOX, ROS), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (TRAF, ASK1, MKK3, MKK4, ERK), as well as the expression of procollagen I (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: At low levels of tension, knockdowns produced only small changes in node activities and correspondingly low influence and sensitivity values.
source: At low levels of tension, knockdowns produced only small changes in node activities and correspondingly low influence and sensitivity values (Figure 4A, D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by perturbation analysis data shown in Figure 4A, D, and E.

claim: Under medium tension levels, knockdown of AT1R exhibited relatively broad inhibition compared to other top influencers, decreasing activity levels of several proMMPs, fibronectin, TNC, and members of the IL6 pathway by an average of 35.9% ± 5.4%.
source: Under medium tension levels, knockdown of AT1R exhibited relatively broad inhibition compared to other top influencers, decreasing activity levels of several proMMPs, fibronectin, TNC, and members of the IL6 pathway by an average of 35.9% ± 5.4% (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by perturbation analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under high-tension conditions, NOX, ROS, AP1, and JNK ranked as the highest influencers network-wide.
source: Under high-tension conditions, however, these four nodes ranked as the highest influencers network-wide, mediating decreases in activity for members of the MAPK pathways (80.6% ± 4.3% reduction in activity on average), actin cytoskeleton-related signaling (68.7% ± 22.2% average reduction), and outputs procollagen I, procollagen III, and proMMP1 (30.9% ± 8.9% average reduction) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by perturbation analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The model independently confirmed that increasing levels of AT1R knockdown combined with NP overexpression further attenuated procollagen I expression compared to AT1R knockdown alone.
source: Von Lueder and colleagues previously found that valsartan primarily attenuated collagen expression in cardiac fibroblasts following exposure to AngII, with NEPi LBQ657 acting in a synergistic manner with valsartan but not altering collagen expression alone (von Lueder et al., 2015). Our model independently confirmed this conclusion, as increasing levels of AT1R knockdown combined with NP overexpression further attenuated procollagen I expression compared to AT1R knockdown alone (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5A that matches experimental findings from von Lueder et al., 2015.

claim: Model simulations predicted a similar synergistic inhibition of αSMA, collagen I, and periostin in high TGFβ1/AngII/atrial NP (T/A/A) conditions.
source: We compared model predictions of three model outputs following ARB or ARB-NEPi treatments to a recent study by Burke and colleagues, who observed synergistic inhibition of genes encoding alpha-smooth muscle actin (αSMA), collagen I, and periostin by combinations of valsartan and the NEPi sacubitril (Burke et al., 2019). We found that model simulations predicted a similar synergistic inhibition of all three gene products in high TGFβ1/AngII/atrial NP (T/A/A) conditions, and although simulations of ARB treatment alone reduced output expression as concluded in the von Lueder study, combinatory treatment in this context further reduced all three model outputs to an average 16.6% of positive controls (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5B that matches experimental findings from Burke et al., 2019.

claim: Comprehensive simulations of fibroblast responses to over 23,000 combinatory drug targets in low- or high-tension contexts identified several drug combinations that adapted fibrotic activity to the local mechanical state.
source: Comprehensive simulations of fibroblast responses to over 23,000 combinatory drug targets in low- or high-tension contexts identified several drug combinations that adapted fibrotic activity to the local mechanical state, demonstrating the potential of this model to act as a screening tool for targeted therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is supported by the computational drug screen described in the abstract and results.

claim: 450 of 23,544 combinatory perturbations qualitatively altered matrix content based on regional tension.
source: While no individual drug target perturbation achieved these opposing responses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), we found that 450 of 23,544 combinatory perturbations qualitatively altered matrix content based on regional tension, and we identified a cluster of 13 perturbations that scored highly in adapting expression of fibrosis-related outputs to regional tension (Figure 6A, boxed combinations).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative results from the drug screen shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 13 perturbations scored highly in adapting expression of fibrosis-related outputs to regional tension.
source: While no individual drug target perturbation achieved these opposing responses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), we found that 450 of 23,544 combinatory perturbations qualitatively altered matrix content based on regional tension, and we identified a cluster of 13 perturbations that scored highly in adapting expression of fibrosis-related outputs to regional tension (Figure 6A, boxed combinations).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative results from the drug screen shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 8 of 13 treatments targeted members of the IL6 and Akt/mTOR signaling pathways.
source: This cluster primarily involved dual knockdown of nodes related to the IL6 and Akt/mTOR signaling pathways, with 8 of 13 treatments targeting members of these pathways (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the top-scoring drug combinations shown in Figures 6B-C.

claim: Four out of six perturbations showed statistically significant differences in the drug treatment effects on collagen content with decreased collagen under low mechanical stimulation and increased collagen content under high mechanical stimulation.
source: In follow-up in vitro experiments, we tested a subset of six combination perturbations by treating primary human cardiac fibroblasts cultured with pharmacological inhibitors under low mechanical stimulation (8 kPa stiffness plates) or high mechanical stimulation (64 kPa stiffness plates). Excitingly, four out of the six perturbations showed statistically significant differences in the drug treatment effects on collagen content (assessed as fluorescence intensity) with decreased collagen under low mechanical stimulation and increased collagen content under high mechanical stimulation (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Increased circumferential stretch and stiffness in the post-MI infarct zone have been established as both a direct regulator of fibroblast activation and an indirect regulator of biochemical signaling pathways via crosstalk mechanisms.
source: Increased circumferential stretch and stiffness in the post-MI infarct zone have been established as both a direct regulator of fibroblast activation and an indirect regulator of biochemical signaling pathways via crosstalk mechanisms (Herum et al., 2017b; Margadant and Sonnenberg, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Herum et al., 2017b and Margadant and Sonnenberg, 2010.

claim: Activation of CREB through the use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors has been shown to antagonize fibrotic expression of lung and cardiac fibroblasts.
source: Activation of CREB through the use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors has previously been shown to antagonize fibrotic expression of lung and cardiac fibroblasts (Miller et al., 2011; Wójcik-Pszczoła et al., 2020) as well as cardiac fibrosis in a pressure overload mouse model (Gong et al., 2014), suggesting a potential mechano-responsiveness of this mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2011 and Wójcik-Pszczoła et al., 2020.

claim: Valvular myofibroblasts exhibited earlier and greater induction of bioactive TGFβ1 and aSMA protein levels when subjected to combined tension/TGFβ1 compared to either stimulus alone.
source: This trend is consistent with experiments involving valvular myofibroblasts, which exhibited earlier and greater induction of bioactive TGFβ1 and aSMA protein levels when subjected to combined tension/TGFβ1 compared to either stimulus alone (Merryman et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Merryman et al., 2007.

claim: In BAMBI-/- mice, pressure overload worsened fibrosis compared to wild-type mice in a TGFβ1-dependent manner.
source: In BAMBI-/- mice, pressure overload worsened fibrosis compared to wild-type mice in a TGFβ1-dependent manner, suggesting that this negative regulation is dependent on both mechanical stress and TGFβ1 stimulation (Villar et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Villar et al., 2013.

claim: IL1 has been shown to reverse the myofibroblast phenotype in valvular interstitial cells with culture on stiff substrates.
source: IL1 has additionally been shown to reverse the myofibroblast phenotype in valvular interstitial cells with culture on stiff substrates (Aguado et al., 2019), further suggesting that context-dependent regulation by IL1 may be a determining factor of fibroblast phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aguado et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibition of NOX2 and NOX4 in AngII-infusion mouse models has been shown to attenuate interstitial collagen deposition.
source: Inhibition of NOX2 and NOX4 in AngII-infusion mouse models has additionally been shown to attenuate interstitial collagen deposition, further implicating NOX/ROS signaling as a central influencer of cardiac fibrosis (Johar et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johar et al., 2006 and Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: Studies inhibiting known mediators of excessive fibrosis such as TGFβ1, osteopontin, and TIMP3 have shown increased risk of left ventricular thinning and cardiac rupture.
source: Studies inhibiting known mediators of excessive fibrosis such as TGFβ1, osteopontin, and TIMP3 have shown increased risk of left ventricular thinning and cardiac rupture, early complications associated with impaired scar formation at the infarct zone (Hammoud et al., 2011; Ikeuchi et al., 2004; Trueblood et al., 2001) – an indication that therapies designed to inhibit global fibrosis are not sufficient to promote healthy scar formation where it is needed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hammoud et al., 2011, Ikeuchi et al., 2004, and Trueblood et al., 2001.

claim: The model was implemented as logic-based ODEs in which activity levels of all nodes were modeled as a system of Hill equations.
source: As previously described (Tan et al., 2017; Zeigler et al., 2016), the final network was implemented as logic-based ODEs in which activity levels of all nodes were modeled as a system of Hill equations, and all activity levels and input stimuli were represented as normalized values between 0 and 1.
evidence: The claim describes the computational methodology used in the study.

claim: A curated body of experimental literature kept separate from model construction was used for validation.
source: A curated body of experimental literature kept separate from model construction was used for validation, and most studies were additionally kept separate from each other in terms of authorship, with only 4 of 47 studies containing repeat authors from a single group and 2 of 47 studies containing a repeat author from a separate group, accounting for 10.2% and 1.7% of the total validation set for each group.
evidence: The claim describes the validation methodology used in the study.

claim: Because studies used for validation conducted in vitro experiments on tissue culture plastic, a tension input weight of 0.4 (40% of maximum stimulation) was used for all validation simulations.
source: Because studies used for validation conducted in vitro experiments on tissue culture plastic, a tension input weight of 0.4 (40% of maximum stimulation) was used for all validation simulations.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological choice based on experimental conditions.

claim: Primary human ventricular cardiac fibroblasts were purchased from Lonza (#CC-2904).
source: Primary human ventricular cardiac fibroblasts were purchased (Lonza #CC-2904) and cultured according to manufacturer's protocols with manufacturer-supplied growth medium (FGM-3 with 10% fetal bovine serum, fibroblast growth factor B, GA-1000).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental materials used in the validation experiments.

claim: Variable stiffness plates (8 kPa vs. 64 kPa CytoSoft Imaging 24-well plates) were purchased from Advanced Biomatrix.
source: For testing drug effects under low mechanical stimulation vs. high mechanical stimulation, variable stiffness plates were purchased (8 kPa vs. 64 kPa CytoSoft Imaging 24-well plates, Advanced Biomatrix) and coated with collagen I according to manufacturer's protocols (PureCol, Advanced Biomatrix).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental materials used in the validation experiments.

claim: Fibroblasts at passages 4–6 were seeded on collagen-coated plates at 25,000 cells per well.
source: Fibroblasts at passages 4–6 were seeded on collagen-coated plates at 25,000 cells per well, cultured in normal growth medium for 24 hr at 37°C and 5% CO2, then treated with one of seven media conditions listed in Table 3.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol used in the validation experiments.

claim: After 72 hr of incubation with treatment media, cells were washed with PBS and stained for collagen I.
source: After 72 hr of incubation with treatment media, cells were washed with PBS and stained for collagen I (Fisher #PA5-95137 primary antibody, Fisher #A-11012 Texas Red secondary antibody) and nuclei (DAPI), then imaged at 20× magnification with an EVOS FL-Auto inverted microscope.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol used in the validation experiments.

claim: A total of 210 images were taken, accounting for seven media conditions × two stiffness conditions × three biological replicates/condition × five technical replicates/biological replicate.
source: A total of 210 images were taken, accounting for seven media conditions × two stiffness conditions × three biological replicates/condition × five technical replicates/biological replicate.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design used in the validation experiments.
